title: User Execution: Malicious Link
summary: Malicious link is the sub-technique of user execution in which the adversary depends on the victim clicking a hyperlink rather than opening a file. The link itself is not the payload; it is a pointer, which is why filtering must judge a destination rather than an attachment. Common outcomes of a click include loading an exploit kit or a crafted page that attacks a browser or plug-in flaw, starting a download of a file that the victim must then run, being redirected through several servers before the real destination appears, and being sent to a fake login page to harvest credentials. The link may arrive by email, chat, a social network message, a text message or a document, and may use a shortening or redirect service so the visible text hides the true host, or a lookalike domain that closely resembles a trusted one. Evidence lives in email and messaging gateway records, in web proxy or secure web gateway logs showing the request and the referral chain, in domain name resolution records for the host, and in the browser download history and file creation events that follow. The reliable discriminator is the sequence: a message carrying a link, a click moments later, a redirect, a download, and a new process starting.

beginner.definition: This means the attacker only needs you to click a link. The link leads to a page that attacks your browser or starts a download. The attacker does not ask you to run anything at first. One click is the whole trick.
beginner.whyItMatters: Links are everywhere in email and chat, so a link is easy to send and easy to trust. The address can look almost like a company you know. It can also pass through a short link that hides where it really goes. Because nothing is attached, email filters have less to inspect.
howItWorks: The attacker sends a message containing a link, often pretending to be a service you use.
The link text looks harmless, but the real address points to the attacker's server.
You click, and your browser asks the domain name system for the address of that server.
The server may redirect you through other sites before the final page loads.
That page attacks a browser flaw, shows a fake login page, or starts a file download.
If a file is downloaded, opening it takes the attack into the next stage.
beginner.example: Imagine a note posted in a shared flat saying the water meter needs checking, with a phone number to call. You call the number and someone asks for your bank details. Nothing was broken and the note was on your own door. The danger was the instruction to follow the link, not the link itself.
takeaways: Check where a link really goes before you click, especially in unexpected messages.
Filtering must understand destinations, not only attachments.
Watch for the pattern of a click followed by a redirect and then a download.

objectives: Explain what this sub-technique adds compared with the parent technique of user execution.
Describe the possible outcomes of clicking a malicious link, including exploitation and credential theft.
Explain how shortened and lookalike addresses hide the true destination.
Identify email gateway, web proxy and domain resolution records that reveal the click path.
Describe why link based attacks are harder to filter than file attachments.
